design_detail: Clinical consensus statement by modified Delphi (the Rosenfeld et al. manual) on diagnosing and managing cocaine-induced midline destructive lesions (CIMDL). Panel: 18 otolaryngologists of the rhinology research group of the Young Otolaryngologists section of IFOS (Yo-IFOS), from Italy, France, Spain, the United Kingdom and Canada, who are also the 18 authors. A search of MEDLINE, EMBASE, Scopus and Web of Science on 19 July 2023 (five languages) kept 23 articles of the kind guidelines, consensus statements, meta-analyses, systematic reviews or randomized trials, and the panel added one; by their titles in the reference list these are mostly narrative reviews, including the authors' own systematic review (Nitro et al., 2022). The chair and vice-chair drafted 44 statements, which were rated anonymously online on a 9-point scale in three rounds, statements short of consensus being reworded between rounds. No patient data.
can_establish: What 18 otolaryngologists from one invited research group agreed on, and how strongly, about defining, diagnosing, investigating, following and treating cocaine-induced midline lesions, including that stopping nasal cocaine use is the only known way to halt them and that repair surgery should wait for 12 months of toxicology-proven abstinence.
cannot_establish: Whether any recommended practice improves outcomes, how often lesions occur, progress, stop or heal after people stop using cocaine, or what people who use cocaine, addiction specialists or maxillofacial and plastic surgeons would recommend: the statements are expert opinion resting mainly on reviews, with no patient data or outcome studies.

sample.recruitment: The Yo-IFOS research group is invitation-only: board-certified otolaryngologists under 45 selected by its scientific committee for the extent and impact of their scientific output, who must complete one proposal and take part in two projects every 24 months to keep membership. 18 voluntary members of its rhinology group formed the panel (p. 3, 2.1). Core team: a chair (V. Favier), a vice-chair (L. Nitro) and a methodologist (A. M. Saibene); two panellists (F. Carsuzaa, M. Fieux) improved the first draft (p. 3).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Panel: members of the group's rhinology section; no addiction medicine, maxillofacial or plastic surgery members, and no patients or people who use drugs (limitations, p. 15). Literature: human data, five languages; by the PRISMA figure, 894 abstracts and 8 full texts were excluded as lower-level evidence than guidelines, consensus statements, meta-analyses, systematic reviews and randomized trials (Figure 1, p. 4).
sample.demographics: Otolaryngologists from five countries in Europe and North America (p. 3; affiliations p. 1). Individual characteristics not reported.
sample.attrition: None: all panellists took part in all three rounds (p. 5).
sample.selection_effects: The panel rated statements drafted by its own leaders; all panellists are authors; two of the three core members wrote the classification the panel endorsed (statement 2.2) and the management scheme is built on it (Figure 2). Only rhinologists voted, and the authors note that external-nose deformity and addiction care lie outside their expertise (p. 15).

exposure.measurement: Not applicable (an opinion survey). The statements concern recreational nasal cocaine use reported by patients or shown by toxicology (statement 1.1, p. 5).
exposure.polysubstance: The limitations say other drug use should be assessed and makes management more complex (p. 16); statements 2.9 and 2.10 cover lesions from other snorted drugs (p. 7).

outcomes.instruments: Ratings from 1 (strongly disagree) to 9 (strongly agree) collected with Google Forms through one-time links and personal identification numbers managed by a coordinator outside the panel; mean, median, range and number of outliers per statement (p. 4, 2.3, 2nd paragraph; Tables 1–5).
outcomes.validity_norms: Thresholds from Rosenfeld et al.: strong consensus, mean at least 8.00 and no outlier (a rating 2 or more points from the mean); consensus, mean at least 7.00 and at most one outlier; near-consensus, mean at least 6.50 and at most two outliers; otherwise no consensus (p. 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Agreement among panellists on each statement; no clinical outcome is measured.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Ratings were anonymous to the panel (p. 4). Statements short of consensus were revised between rounds from anonymous comments (p. 5); the record of how each statement changed (Appendix A) is announced but not printed in the file read (p. 16).

analysis.effect_sizes: Round 1: of 44 statements, 4 strong consensus, 9 consensus, 16 near-consensus, 15 no consensus; round 2 (31 revised statements): 5, 6, 10 and 10; round 3 (20 statements): 11, 5, 3 and 1; final: 20 strong consensus, 20 consensus, 3 near-consensus, 1 no consensus (p. 5). Final means of adopted statements range from 7.44 (statement 1.1, the definition) to 8.89 (statement 3.4, no safe threshold) (Tables 1–4); the lowest single rating was 1 for three statements (1.1, 2.10 and the near-consensus 1.4).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No registration or published protocol is mentioned; the method follows the Rosenfeld et al. manual (ref. 9). Ethics committee decision n° 2024-03-035-VF (p. 3).
analysis.selective_reporting: Only final-round values are tabulated; the progression of statements across rounds is said to be in Appendix A, which the file does not contain. Statements that failed to reach consensus are listed with their scores (Table 5).

interpretation_gap.results_show: After rewording, 18 rhinologists from one research group reached at least consensus on 40 of 44 statements: on investigation (what to ask about, when to biopsy, which blood tests and imaging), on first-line care (saline rinses and emollients, debridement of crusts, antibiotics only for infection, avoiding strong opioids, offering addiction medicine, obturators for palatal holes), on follow-up, and on surgery (repair only after 12 months of toxicology-proven abstinence). They agreed strongly that patients should be told no amount of cocaine is a safe threshold for these lesions and that stopping is the only known way to halt them. They did not reach consensus on reconstruction techniques, on drug testing people who deny use, on drug-test detection windows, or on excluding medical cocaine as a cause.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the panel international and “multidisciplinary” (p. 2), but the methods and limitations describe members of one rhinology research group and a study involving rhinologists only (pp. 3, 15). The conclusion of the abstract says the statement establishes a management framework and significantly bridges a knowledge gap (p. 2), while the discussion acknowledges the scarcity of solid evidence (p. 12) and the limitations call the study subjective (p. 15). The statements most relevant to people who use cocaine are opinion: no safe threshold and stopping as the only way to halt the disease cite one narrative review (ref. 31, p. 15); the 12-month wait before repair is borrowed from the DSM-5 definition of sustained remission, with an uncited sentence that relapse risk falls with longer abstinence (p. 15). None of the statements carries a grade of the evidence behind it.

timeline.event: Trimarchi et al. case series on telling CIMDL from Wegener granulomatosis (not among this statement's 24 articles, which kept reviews and higher-level designs only)

Nitro et al. systematic review and four-grade classification, written by this panel's vice-chair and methodologist with others; adopted by the panel (statement 2.2) and used for the management scheme (Figure 2)

replication.where_it_stands: An expert consensus without patient data. It cites no study testing its recommendations; the authors call for none specifically but note that reconstruction techniques rest on anecdotal literature and that hyperbaric oxygen needs further evidence (p. 15).

funding.funder: This research received no external funding (p. 16).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest (p. 16; also stated in the methods, p. 3).
funding.affiliations_note: University and hospital otolaryngology departments in Milan, Poitiers, Paris, Strasbourg, Valencia, Santander, Enna, Marseille, London (Ontario), Truro, Jerez, Nice, Montpellier and Lyon (p. 1). All 18 panellists are the authors. L. Nitro and A. M. Saibene, vice-chair and methodologist, are first and senior authors of the systematic review and classification the panel adopted (ref. 5); A. M. Saibene co-wrote a case report the statement cites for skull-base complications (ref. 38). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the statement.

what_would_settle_it: Prospective follow-up of people with cocaine-related nasal lesions who stop or continue using, with endoscopy and imaging at set intervals and toxicology, and comparative studies of rinses, debridement, palatal obturators and the timing and technique of repair, with outcomes that matter to patients (breathing, crusting, bleeding, pain, appearance, failed repair).

domains.note: Four databases, a stated search string and date, and a PRISMA figure; but the selection rule kept only reviews and higher-level designs, so the primary case series (the main evidence on these lesions) were excluded, the PRISMA reasons for full-text exclusion do not add up, and statements are not linked to the articles that support them.
No appraisal of the 24 articles is reported; the authors describe most as descriptive level 4 or 5 studies without a control group (p. 3).

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The panel endorsed, and built its management scheme on, the classification published by its vice-chair and methodologist (statement 2.2; Figure 2); most other statements do not depend on the authors' own studies.

Statements are worded as instructions (patients must be advised; a CT is recommended) without any grading of the evidence behind each; opinions such as no safe threshold are presented as facts patients should be correctly informed of (p. 8), supported by one review citation (p. 15).

domains.domain: Balance of perspectives: otolaryngology against addiction medicine, other surgical specialties and people who use cocaine
domains.note: Only rhinologists voted (p. 15); addiction specialists, maxillofacial and plastic surgeons and people with lived experience are absent, and the limitations use stigmatizing labels for people who use drugs (p. 16), at odds with the statement's own advice to refer patients to addiction medicine.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a consensus statement; the project's narrative-review checklist is used, as the round brief directs. The Delphi process itself was orderly (anonymous ratings, stated thresholds, no attrition), but the evidence base was not appraised, primary case series were excluded by design, statements are ungraded, and the panel is one specialty rating drafts by its own leaders. Citable for: what this panel of rhinologists recommends and how strongly they agreed (statement numbers and scores), for example stopping nasal cocaine use as the only known way to halt lesions, a 12-month toxicology-confirmed wait before repair, saline rinses and debridement for crusting, obturators for palatal holes, and investigations for people who deny use or whose lesions grow after stopping. Not citable for: how often lesions occur, progress or heal, or for the effectiveness of any treatment.

key_findings.finding: 18 Yo-IFOS rhinologists rated 44 statements in three rounds, all taking part in every round; after rewording, 20 statements reached strong consensus, 20 consensus, 3 near-consensus and 1 no consensus (round 1 alone: 4 strong consensus, 9 consensus, 16 near-consensus, 15 none).

Definition: CIMDL is any structural lesion of the sinonasal complex in a person with a cocaine-snorting habit confirmed by history or toxicology screening (statement 1.1, consensus, mean 7.44, median 7.5, range 1–9, the lowest-rated adopted statement); it covers palatal as well as sinonasal lesions (1.2, strong consensus, mean 8.83); diagnosis should not rely on autoantibody tests, which can be positive or negative (1.3, strong consensus, mean 8.50). The discussion presents the one-lesion definition as replacing older positions that required at least two lesions.

Telling CIMDL from other diseases: the differential list includes vasculitis such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis, T-cell or NK/T lymphoma, infections (syphilis, leishmaniasis, yaws, leprosy, tuberculosis, actinomycosis), Crohn's disease, long-term use of vasoconstrictor drugs, compulsive nose picking, trauma, other snorted drugs, IgG4-related disease, relapsing polychondritis, rhinoscleroma, sclerosing orbital pseudotumour and medical causes (2.3, consensus, mean 8.50). For an isolated septal perforation, cocaine snorting should be asked about together with trauma, earlier nasal procedures (including radiotherapy and nasal oxygen), long-term nasal vasoconstrictors, picking or foreign bodies, infections and autoimmune disease or vasculitis (2.4, strong consensus, 8.67); if no cause is found, a biopsy and personalised follow-up should be considered (2.5, strong consensus, 8.33). People with a possible grade II or worse lesion and no history of cocaine snorting should have a full workup with blood tests, specialist referral and nasal biopsy (2.6, consensus, 7.78).
key_findings.note: The discussion adds that any crusted lesion of the nasal mucosa may be cancer and that sinonasal lymphoma can be hard to diagnose even on biopsy (p. 14).

key_findings.finding: Lesions that grow after stopping: people who report having stopped completely but whose lesions increase at follow-up should have a full workup with blood tests, specialist consultation and biopsy (2.13, strong consensus, mean 8.56), and a drug test can be considered (2.14, consensus, mean 8.22). Growing isolated septal perforations in people without CIMDL should also have a full workup (2.12, strong consensus, 8.67).
key_findings.note: The panel thus treats growth after stopping as unexpected and a reason to look for another cause or continued use; no data on the course after stopping are given.

key_findings.finding: The two highest-rated statements: patients should be correctly informed that no “safe threshold” of cocaine use prevents further evolution of the lesions (3.4, strong consensus, mean 8.89, range 8–9) and must be advised that the only known way to halt lesion development is to stop nasal cocaine use (3.3, strong consensus, mean 8.61). The discussion supports both with one narrative review (ref. 31).

First-line care: daily saline rinses for nasal hygiene and emollients against crusting (3.12, consensus, mean 8.44); antibiotics only for bacterial superinfection or osteitis, with bone cultures where possible (3.13, strong consensus, 8.72); endoscopic removal of crusts and dead tissue or high-volume rinses to ease blockage and foul smell (3.14, strong consensus, 8.72); palatal obturator prostheses as first-line care for a palatal perforation (3.15, consensus, 8.11); offering a specialist in addiction medicine (3.1, consensus, 8.39); avoiding strong opioids for pain and involving addiction or pain services if pain is uncontrolled (3.2, strong consensus, 8.67).

Imaging and complications: a baseline plain CT of the sinuses, orbits and skull base for grade II or worse (3.9, strong consensus, 8.56); contrast only for suspected osteitis or osteonecrosis (3.8, consensus, 8.00); MRI only for orbital, skull-base, intracranial or soft-tissue involvement (3.10, strong consensus, 8.44); people with grade III or worse should be told the warning signs of orbital or skull-base complications and to seek emergency care promptly (3.7, consensus, 8.17); pneumococcal, Haemophilus and meningococcal vaccines for grade IV (3.16, consensus, 8.22).
key_findings.note: Item 3.10 is printed as 3.1 in the table.

key_findings.finding: Follow-up: personalised by grade, with more frequent visits to encourage stopping; in stable patients every 6 to 12 months for up to 2 to 5 years after stopping cocaine snorting (3.17, strong consensus, mean 8.28).

Repair: septal, nasal and palatal reconstruction should not be done unless the person is well motivated and proves stopping with toxicology covering at least 12 months (4.7, consensus, mean 8.61, range 5–9, 1 outlier). The 12 months follow the DSM-5 start of sustained remission; the discussion adds, without a citation, that relapse risk falls with longer abstinence. Reconstruction techniques reached only near-consensus (4.8, mean 7.94, 2 outliers), the literature on them being described as anecdotal; hyperbaric oxygen is called an option needing further evidence.
key_findings.locator: Table 4, item 4.7 (p. 11); Table 5, item 4.8 (p. 12); 4.4, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Severe complications: intraorbital complications first treated with culture-guided antibiotics, with endoscopic drainage for a sudden drop in visual acuity or loss of colour perception, large or superior or lateral abscesses, or failed medical therapy (4.3, strong consensus, 8.44); grade IV without cerebrospinal fluid leak or intracranial complication managed conservatively (4.4, strong consensus, 8.72); with a leak, debridement and prompt skull-base reconstruction (4.5, strong consensus, 8.67).

Not agreed: that CIMDL arises only from recreational and never from medical nasal cocaine (1.4, near-consensus, mean 7.61, removed); that people with suspected CIMDL who deny use and have a negative workup should have a cocaine test (2.7, no consensus, mean 7.83, 3 outliers); that recreational use can be shown by urine metabolites 3 to 15 days after use or by hair analysis up to 3 months (2.8, near-consensus, mean 8.28).

On healing after past use, the discussion states that in someone who used in previous years but not recently, an isolated septal perforation with good healing (no crusting or inflammation) could suggest CIMDL, whereas active inflammation or crusting calls for further investigation and a differential diagnosis. No data on how often or how fast lesions settle after stopping are given.

Evidence base: 1047 records screened, 45 full texts, 23 articles kept plus 1 added by the panel; 894 abstracts and 8 full texts were excluded as lower-level evidence than guidelines, consensus statements, meta-analyses, systematic reviews and randomized trials. The authors state that most kept articles were descriptive level 4 or 5 studies without a control group, so that a systematic review could not be performed.
key_findings.locator: 2.2 Systematic Literature Review, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 3); Figure 1 (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: the subjective nature of the method; only rhinologists, so deformities of the nasal dorsum, nasal pyramid and lips were not assessed; otolaryngologists are not experts in addiction; most people do not disclose their use and relapses are frequent.

reporting_issues.issue: Statement 2.2 (the Nitro et al. classification) is printed with 0 outliers but a minimum rating of 5 against a mean of 8.44, which by the paper's own definition (a rating 2 or more points from the mean) is an outlier; with 0 outliers and a mean above 8.00 it would have been strong consensus, yet it is labelled consensus.
reporting_issues.consequence: The outlier count or the label is wrong; the label fits at least one outlier.

reporting_issues.issue: Statement 4.1 (rhinosinusitis treated as per EPOS/ICAR guidelines) has 2 outliers but is labelled consensus, although the stated rule allows at most one outlier for consensus; by that rule it is near-consensus.
reporting_issues.consequence: The final totals would be 19 consensus and 4 near-consensus rather than 20 and 3 (editors' application of the stated rule).

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says the two lowest-scoring items (1.4 and 1.1) both had a median of 7.5; Table 5 gives statement 1.4 a median of 9 (Table 1 gives 1.1 a median of 7.5).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; one of the two medians is misreported.

reporting_issues.issue: The results text says 29 of 44 items had a median of 9; the final-round values in Tables 1–5 give a median of 9 for 41 of 44 (all but 1.1, 2.9 and 3.5; editors' count).
reporting_issues.consequence: The text figure may refer to an earlier round, but as printed it contradicts the tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The PRISMA figure gives 22 full texts excluded, but its listed reasons add up to 21 (8, 1, 1, 2 and 9).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor arithmetic error in the flow chart.

reporting_issues.issue: Appendix A, said to show how each statement evolved across the three rounds, has its heading and colour legend but no content in the file read.
reporting_issues.consequence: The wording rated in rounds 1 and 2 and the effect of rewording on agreement cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: Item numbers 2.10 and 3.10 are printed as 2.1 and 3.1, duplicating existing numbers; statements 2.7 and 2.8 appear only in Table 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: Statements should be cited by table position or wording as well as number.

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Figure 2 begins as a PRISMA flow chart of the literature, but the figure shows the management scheme by grade.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typesetting error; the figure content is the management overview.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes an international multidisciplinary panel; the methods describe members of one rhinology research group and the limitations a study only involving rhinologists.
reporting_issues.consequence: The panel's breadth is overstated in the abstract.

reporting_issues.issue: The two rhinologists who improved the first draft are said to have been randomly chosen among panellists and, in the next sentence, to have joined voluntarily or been recommended as experts.
reporting_issues.consequence: How the drafting team was chosen is unclear.

reporting_issues.issue: The informed consent statement says written consent was obtained from the patient(s) to publish, while the institutional review board statement says the study involves no human data.
reporting_issues.consequence: Boilerplate inconsistency; no patient data are reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The introduction cites Nitro et al. (2022) for cocaine snorting significantly affecting patients' quality of life; that review, read in this session, reports no quality-of-life data.
reporting_issues.consequence: A citation that does not support the statement it is attached to.

reporting_issues.issue: The methods say the review was broadened to include randomized trials and the PRISMA figure excludes everything below guidelines, consensus statements, meta-analyses, systematic reviews and trials, yet the methods also say most included articles were descriptive level 4 or 5 studies; by their titles the 24 articles are mostly narrative reviews and none is a trial.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence the panel was given is second-hand: reviews of the case series rather than the series themselves.
